explanation: Aniridic glaucoma arises from progressive apposition of the rudimentary iris stump over the trabecular meshwork, and once maximal medical therapy fails the eye needs a filtering or drainage procedure. Trabeculectomy with mitomycin C is the only surgical option offered and is a recognised choice, although many surgeons prefer a glaucoma drainage device in these eyes because the abnormal anterior segment and young age give high bleb-failure rates. Adding another beta blocker is futile when the child is already uncontrolled on medication, laser trabeculoplasty is ineffective and essentially contraindicated in a developmentally abnormal angle without a visible pigmented meshwork, and observation risks irreversible optic nerve damage. Prophylactic goniotomy of the angle is a preventive strategy in aniridia but does not apply once glaucoma is established and medically uncontrolled.

Primary congenital glaucoma results from maldevelopment of the angle, and gonioscopy classically shows a high, flat anterior insertion of the iris root directly into the trabecular meshwork with loss of the normal angle recess and a translucent tissue sheen. Iridocorneal adhesions and posterior embryotoxon belong to the Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum, which is a different anterior segment dysgenesis with prominent iris and corneal findings. A Sampaolesi line is a wavy pigmented band anterior to Schwalbe line seen in pseudoexfoliation and pigment dispersion, both acquired adult conditions.

Goldmann applanation assumes an average corneal thickness and rigidity; an oedematous cornea is soft and easily flattened, so the measured pressure underestimates true intraocular pressure. Corneal scarring and increased rigidity stiffen the tissue and make the eye harder to applanate, producing a falsely high reading. Excess fluorescein widens the mires and makes the examiner reduce the dial force too late, again overestimating pressure, and inadequate fluorescein is what produces a falsely low reading from thin mires.

A long-standing mature or hypermature cataract with an intact capsule leaks high molecular weight lens protein through microscopic capsular defects; macrophages engorged with this protein obstruct an anatomically open trabecular meshwork, giving acute pain, very high pressure and only mild cell and flare without keratic precipitates. Phacoantigenic uveitis requires a breach of the lens capsule from trauma or surgery and produces a granulomatous reaction with mutton-fat keratic precipitates and synechiae. Fuchs uveitis gives diffuse stellate keratic precipitates with a quiet white eye rather than acute pain, and Posner-Schlossman causes recurrent very high pressure with fine non-pigmented precipitates in an otherwise normal lens.

The hypertensive phase of tube shunt surgery typically appears between three and eight weeks postoperatively and is caused by fibrous encapsulation and thickening of the bleb wall over the extraocular plate, which raises resistance to aqueous outflow. The timing is the giveaway, as it corresponds to the peak of the fibroblastic healing response around the reservoir. Steroid response and persistent inflammation can raise pressure but are far less common as the dominant mechanism at this interval and would usually be accompanied by a suggestive slit lamp picture, and progression of the underlying glaucoma does not cause an abrupt pressure rise weeks after surgery.

A central corneal thickness of 620 microns causes Goldmann to substantially overestimate true intraocular pressure, so the real pressure in this patient is likely in the high teens to low twenties. With a healthy neural rim, a symmetric cup-disc ratio of 0.5 and thick corneas, this is low-risk ocular hypertension, and the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study identified thin rather than thick corneas as the major predictor of conversion. Observation with baseline fields, imaging and periodic review is appropriate, whereas committing to lifelong drops or surgery is not justified by these numbers alone.

An anterior chamber intraocular lens sits in front of the iris and predisposes to pupillary block, so a peripheral iridectomy must be created at the time of surgery rather than being deferred to a postoperative laser. It is placed superiorly at 12 o'clock so the upper lid covers it and the patient does not suffer glare or a second image through the opening. Waiting for a laser iridotomy leaves the eye at risk of an acute block in the early postoperative period, and an inferior position is reserved for silicone oil filled eyes where the oil rises and would occlude a superior opening.

The Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial showed that each 1 mmHg of intraocular pressure reduction was associated with roughly a 10 percent reduction in the risk of glaucomatous progression. This underpins the everyday counselling that even modest pressure lowering is worthwhile and that there is no threshold below which further lowering stops helping. The other figures overstate or understate the effect and do not correspond to any of the major randomised pressure-lowering trials.

In an eye that has harboured an intraocular malignancy, a filtering procedure or a drainage tube creates a transscleral fistula that can seed tumour cells into the subconjunctival space and orbit, so both trabeculectomy and a tube are avoided. Cyclodestruction is performed through intact sclera without creating an outflow track, which makes transscleral cyclophotocoagulation the safest pressure-lowering surgery in this setting. Laser trabeculoplasty is ineffective in the neovascular or angle-infiltrated angles that follow tumour treatment or plaque brachytherapy.
concern: The recall does not state which malignancy or how the eye was treated. If the vignette instead means a systemic cancer treated with corticosteroids, this would be steroid-induced glaucoma and a drainage device would be reasonable. My answer assumes an intraocular tumour, which is the only reading that makes cyclophotocoagulation clearly preferable in an eye still seeing 20/100.

explanation: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus iridocyclitis in an immunocompetent patient is treated with a topical corticosteroid to control the intraocular inflammation together with a systemic antiviral such as oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir, since no topical agent achieves useful intraocular levels against varicella zoster virus. Trifluridine and other topical antivirals are indicated for herpes simplex epithelial keratitis and have no meaningful activity against zoster. Systemic corticosteroids are reserved for severe disease such as optic neuropathy, orbital inflammation or intractable neuritis, not for isolated anterior uveitis.

A solitary focal yellow-white retinal or subretinal lesion with dense overlying vitritis is the classic headlight-in-the-fog appearance of toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis, usually reactivating at the edge of an old pigmented chorioretinal scar. Acute retinal necrosis produces peripheral confluent areas of retinal whitening with occlusive arteriolitis that spread circumferentially and progress rapidly, not a single subretinal focus. Behcet disease causes an occlusive retinal vasculitis with haemorrhage and often a transient hypopyon, and is typically bilateral with systemic mucocutaneous features.

A rash over preceding months followed by anterior chamber inflammation and optic disc swelling is secondary syphilis with ocular involvement, and any ocular syphilis is managed as neurosyphilis with intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G for ten to fourteen days, with topical steroid for the anterior segment and mandatory partner notification and treatment. Doxycycline is an alternative only for uncomplicated early syphilis in penicillin-allergic patients and does not reliably achieve treponemicidal levels in the central nervous system or eye. Corticosteroid alone would treat the inflammation while allowing the spirochaetal infection to progress.

Diffuse small stellate keratic precipitates scattered over the whole endothelium, minimal cells, absence of posterior synechiae, iris hypochromia in the affected eye, early cataract and mildly raised pressure make up the classic picture of Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis. The absence of synechiae despite chronic inflammation is a particularly useful discriminator. Phacolytic and phacoantigenic glaucoma both require an advanced or disrupted lens as the inciting event and neither produces iris heterochromia or stellate precipitates.

Multiple flat cream-coloured placoid lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium confined to the posterior pole in a young adult with photopsias is acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy, which is usually bilateral, often follows a viral illness and typically recovers spontaneously. Serpiginous choroiditis starts peripapillary and extends in a snake-like geographic pattern with recurrences and permanent atrophy, usually in older patients. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada produces bilateral serous retinal detachments with disc hyperaemia and systemic auditory, neurological or integumentary signs, and toxoplasmosis gives a single focal necrotising lesion with vitritis.

A vitrectomised aphakic or pseudophakic eye has lost the vitreous scaffold and much of the normal resistance to aqueous egress, so early overfiltration with hypotony, shallow chamber and choroidal effusion is the commonest problem after drainage implant surgery in this setting. Malignant glaucoma is essentially excluded once the eye has had a complete vitrectomy, since aqueous misdirection depends on an intact vitreous body. Suprachoroidal haemorrhage is a feared but uncommon consequence of hypotony rather than the most frequent event, and tube occlusion in this eye would be expected mainly if residual silicone oil remained, which it does not after oil removal.
concern: The source explanation field for this item contains a stray fragment of a different question about neuroretinitis in a child, which is a transcription artifact rather than an explanation. Non-valved implants are also usually ligated precisely to avoid this complication, so the answer depends on the device assumed.

explanation: Painless vision loss with disc oedema, reduced colour vision and a relative afferent defect in a patient in the fifth or sixth decade is most consistent with non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, which typically shows segmental or diffuse disc swelling on a crowded disc with a small or absent cup and an altitudinal field defect. Optic neuritis at this age is less common, usually causes pain on eye movement and has a normal disc in about two thirds of cases because the lesion is retrobulbar. Giant cell arteritis characteristically affects patients over seventy, produces chalky pallid disc swelling with more profound acuity loss and systemic symptoms, and infiltrative optic neuropathy is rare and usually accompanied by a known malignancy or other neurological signs.
concern: The answer depends on the disc photograph and field, which I cannot see. If the photograph showed pallid rather than hyperaemic swelling, or the vignette contained jaw claudication or scalp tenderness, arteritic disease would take precedence.

explanation: A superonasal defect in the right eye and a superotemporal defect in the left eye together constitute a left superior homonymous quadrantanopia, since the left hemifield is nasal for the right eye and temporal for the left. Superior quadrantic homonymous loss arises either from Meyer loop in the temporal lobe or from the inferior bank of the calcarine fissure in the occipital lobe, and with temporal lobe absent from the list the occipital lobe is the correct choice. Parietal lesions damage the superior optic radiations and produce an inferior quadrantanopia, optic tract lesions cause a markedly incongruous complete hemianopia with a contralateral afferent pupillary defect, and lateral geniculate lesions give the distinctive horizontal or quadruple sectoranopia patterns.
concern: The classic teaching phrase pie in the sky points to the temporal lobe, which is not offered. A highly congruous quadrantanopia favours occipital cortex, so the option list is answerable but the recall has clearly lost the intended distractor.

explanation: Subacute unilateral vision loss with dyschromatopsia and a normal fundus in a young woman is retrobulbar optic neuritis, and paraesthesia points to a demyelinating process. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits with gadolinium is the essential next step because the number of white matter lesions determines the risk of conversion to multiple sclerosis and drives the decision to treat and to start disease-modifying therapy. Intravenous methylprednisolone only speeds recovery and does not change final acuity, and in the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial oral prednisone alone increased recurrences, so steroids should follow rather than precede imaging. Aquaporin-4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies and lumbar puncture are appropriate adjuncts, particularly for atypical or bilateral cases, but do not replace imaging as the first investigation.

Visual acuity in optic nerve hypoplasia is famously unpredictable and spans the full range from normal to no useful vision, because function depends on whether the surviving axons include the papillomacular bundle rather than on the size of the disc. The wide range option therefore captures the teaching point, while the narrow ranges imply a predictable deficit that does not exist in this condition. A disc that appears small with a surrounding pigmented double ring sign should prompt evaluation for midline central nervous system defects and pituitary dysfunction rather than prognostication from disc size alone.
concern: The item hinges on a fundus photograph I cannot see; I am relying on the source note that it depicts optic nerve hypoplasia. Strictly, acuity in this condition ranges from 20/20 to no light perception, so the offered option stopping at light perception is an approximation.

explanation: Elevation of the lid on attempted downgaze is the pseudo-von Graefe sign of aberrant regeneration of the third cranial nerve, in which fibres destined for the medial or inferior rectus misroute to the levator. Aberrant regeneration without a preceding acute painful palsy implies a slowly compressive lesion in the cavernous sinus such as a meningioma or aneurysm, so neuroimaging is mandatory. Intermittent diplopia, fatigability with bulbar symptoms and a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation all point to myasthenia gravis, which is diagnosed serologically and electrophysiologically and prompts chest imaging for thymoma rather than brain imaging.

A presumed microvascular sixth nerve palsy in a vasculopathic patient should be stable or improving by six to twelve weeks; worsening of the deviation is a red flag for a compressive, inflammatory or infiltrative lesion along the nerve. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, including the skull base and cavernous sinus, is the study of choice because it resolves the subarachnoid course, Dorello canal and cavernous sinus far better than computed tomography. Inflammatory markers are appropriate when giant cell arteritis is suspected but this presentation is not that, and simply optimising diabetes and hypertension ignores a progressing neurological sign.

Recent weight gain in a young woman with transient visual obscurations provoked by standing or bending and bilateral disc oedema is idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure is by definition papilledema. The obscurations reflect momentary axonal conduction failure when perfusion pressure at the swollen disc drops with postural change. A posterior optic neuropathy is retrobulbar by definition and cannot produce a swollen disc, so it is internally inconsistent with the photograph. Confirmation still requires neuroimaging with venography and then lumbar puncture with an opening pressure.

Brief episodes of visual blurring lasting about a minute in a man of seventy-eight are transient ischaemic events until proven otherwise, and the two conditions that must not be missed are giant cell arteritis and carotid or cardioembolic disease. The broad workup covers both by obtaining erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein alongside carotid and cardiac evaluation, which is the correct sequence since inflammatory markers precede and justify a temporal artery biopsy. Going straight to biopsy commits the patient to a procedure before any screening result, and observation in a patient at high stroke risk is unsafe. If the inflammatory markers are raised, high-dose steroids should be started immediately and biopsy arranged without waiting.

Acute painful Horner syndrome after trauma, with ipsilateral head or neck pain and ptosis, is internal carotid artery dissection until proven otherwise, because the sympathetic fibres travel on the carotid adventitia. This is a stroke emergency, so urgent computed tomographic angiography of the head and neck in the emergency department is required to confirm the dissection and start antithrombotic therapy. Deferring imaging by a week or referring for a routine outpatient appointment risks a devastating embolic stroke in the interval during which dissections most commonly embolise.

Type 1 Duane syndrome combines limited abduction with esotropia and a compensatory face turn toward the affected side, and upshoot in adduction results from a taut lateral rectus slipping over the globe as the co-contracting muscles tighten. Recessing the ipsilateral medial rectus reduces the esotropia and the head turn, while Y-splitting the lateral rectus broadens its insertion and stops the muscle belly from riding over the globe, addressing the upshoot. Bilateral medial rectus recession alone leaves the upshoot untreated, and lateral rectus resection is contraindicated in Duane because it worsens globe retraction and the aberrant co-contraction.

Morning glory disc anomaly is a funnel-shaped excavated disc with a central glial tuft and radiating vessels, and its important systemic associations are transsphenoidal basal encephalocele, midline craniofacial defects and moyamoya-type cerebrovascular disease, so neuroimaging is warranted. Polydactyly points to Bardet-Biedl syndrome, preauricular skin tags to oculo-auriculo-vertebral or branchio-oto-renal spectrum, and joint hypermobility to connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos, none of which relate to this disc anomaly.

Reading the measurements in the usual cross layout, the exotropia is 20 prism dioptres in upgaze, 45 in primary and lateral gazes and 55 in downgaze, which is an A-pattern exotropia with a 35 prism dioptre difference between up and down. Patients adopt the head posture that places the eyes in the field of least deviation, and here that field is upgaze, which is achieved by depressing the chin. A chin-up posture would place the eyes in downgaze where the deviation is worst, and a horizontal face turn or head tilt would be adopted for an incomitant horizontal or cyclovertical deviation rather than an A pattern.
concern: The recall gives five bare numbers without labelling the gaze positions. My answer assumes the conventional cross notation with upgaze first and downgaze last; a different ordering would change the pattern and hence the posture.

explanation: A consecutive exotropia while wearing the full cycloplegic hyperopic correction means the glasses are now over-correcting for the child's actual accommodative demand, and the appropriate step is to reduce the plus in a stepwise fashion until the eyes are aligned or a small esophoria returns. Bifocals add plus for near and would drive the exotropia further, which is the opposite of what is needed. Prisms treat a residual deviation but do not address the cause here, and observing a symptomatic 10 prism dioptre exotropia risks loss of fusion and amblyopia in a ten-year-old.

A small residual esotropia of about 6 prism dioptres with good acuity after strabismus surgery describes monofixation syndrome, in which there is a central suppression scotoma in one eye with intact peripheral fusion. At distance the Worth four dot targets subtend a small angle and fall entirely within that central scotoma, so the patient suppresses and reports two or three dots, whereas at near the dots subtend a large angle that extends beyond the scotoma into peripherally fusing retina, so all four are seen. Seeing four dots at both distances would indicate normal bifoveal fusion, five dots indicates diplopia, and the reverse pattern of fusion at distance with suppression at near does not fit the anatomy of a central scotoma.

In dextroelevation the right eye is abducted and the left eye is adducted. The superior rectus is the pure elevator when the eye is abducted about 23 degrees, so it raises the right eye, while the inferior oblique is the pure elevator when the eye is adducted about 51 degrees, so it raises the left eye. Yoked muscles must move both eyes in the same direction, and pairing a right elevator with a left depressor such as the inferior rectus describes antagonists rather than yoke muscles.

Postaxial polydactyly, truncal obesity and a rod-cone dystrophy with attenuated vessels and a blunted foveal reflex are the cardinal features of Bardet-Biedl syndrome, a ciliopathy that also causes renal anomalies, learning difficulty and hypogonadism. Alstrom syndrome shares obesity and a cone-rod dystrophy with sensorineural deafness and insulin resistance but never polydactyly. Joubert syndrome is characterised by the molar tooth sign on imaging with hypotonia, abnormal breathing and oculomotor apraxia, and Laurence-Moon is distinguished by spastic paraplegia without polydactyly.

A small consecutive exotropia of about 10 prism dioptres two weeks after esotropia surgery is common and usually settles as the postoperative drift toward exotropia continues to stabilise over the following weeks to months, so reassurance and continued observation are correct. Reoperating at two weeks would be premature and risks over-correcting a deviation that is still changing. Bifocals have no role in a consecutive exotropia, and if the deviation persists beyond a few months, prisms or surgery can be reconsidered then.
concern: The recall writes BLR for a procedure done for esotropia, which is internally inconsistent since esotropia is treated with bilateral medial rectus recession. The management answer is the same either way.

explanation: Strabismus is the second most common presenting sign of retinoblastoma after leukocoria, and an asymmetric or dull red reflex demands a dilated fundus examination, under anaesthesia if necessary, to exclude a retinal or media abnormality. The red reflex abnormality localises the problem to the eye itself, so ocular examination and B-scan ultrasound come before any cross-sectional imaging. Computed tomography is specifically avoided as a first-line study in children with suspected retinoblastoma because of ionising radiation in a population that may carry a germline RB1 mutation.

Orbital lymphangioma is a non-encapsulated venolymphatic malformation prone to spontaneous intralesional haemorrhage, and the resulting blood products settle to give the characteristic fluid-fluid levels within multiloculated cystic spaces on computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. Flow voids indicate high-flow lesions such as arteriovenous malformations or fistulas, homogeneous progressive enhancement of a well-encapsulated mass suggests a cavernous venous malformation, and calcification within the orbit points to lesions such as meningioma or retinoblastoma rather than a lymphangioma.

Thyroid eye disease involves the extraocular muscles in the order inferior rectus, medial rectus, superior rectus and lateral rectus, so the inferior rectus is the most commonly and most severely affected. A fibrotic tight inferior rectus tethers the globe downward, producing hypotropia with limited elevation, and the accompanying upper lid retraction with superior scleral show completes the picture. Lateral and medial rectus restriction would give horizontal rather than vertical misalignment, and isolated superior rectus disease is uncommon and would produce hypertropia rather than hypotropia.

When the clinical picture already describes thyroid eye disease, with proptosis, conjunctival injection and firm resistance to retropulsion, the first investigation is thyroid function testing including thyroid stimulating hormone, free thyroxine and thyroid receptor antibodies, because establishing and correcting the thyroid status is fundamental to the diagnosis and to management. Orbital computed tomography is important but is directed at questions that arise later, namely apical crowding and compressive optic neuropathy, atypical or unilateral presentations, and surgical planning for decompression. Brain magnetic resonance imaging adds nothing to an orbital problem, and acetylcholine receptor antibodies are for coexisting myasthenia, which should be considered because it associates with Graves disease but is not the first test here.
concern: I disagree with the source answer of orbital computed tomography, though only moderately, and the source itself records being undecided between imaging and thyroid function tests. The governing principle is that a clinically classic thyroid eye disease presentation is confirmed serologically first, with imaging reserved for diagnostic doubt or for assessing optic nerve compression. If the vignette actually described unilateral proptosis without other thyroid features, imaging would legitimately come first.

explanation: A well-circumscribed encapsulated intraconal mass in an adult that has been present for years and grows slowly is a cavernous venous malformation, still widely called cavernous haemangioma, which is the most common benign orbital tumour of adulthood and characteristically enlarges during pregnancy under hormonal influence. Capillary haemangioma is a lesion of infancy that presents in the first weeks of life, grows for months and then involutes, and is usually superficial or anterior. Lymphangioma is an ill-defined infiltrative childhood malformation that presents with sudden proptosis from haemorrhage rather than as a discrete encapsulated intraconal mass.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is an angioinvasive fungal infection with high mortality, and survival depends on immediate systemic liposomal amphotericin B combined with urgent surgical debridement of all necrotic sinus and orbital tissue together with correction of the underlying immunosuppression or ketoacidosis. Because the fungus invades along vessels, antifungal drug alone cannot reach devitalised tissue, which is why coordinated ear nose and throat debridement is part of the answer. Enucleation removes the globe but leaves the infected orbit and apex untreated, and decompression alone does not remove necrotic tissue; exenteration is considered only when disease progresses despite maximal medical and debridement therapy.

Levator function is the single most important determinant of ptosis surgery, and poor function of roughly 4 mm or less means the levator cannot be made to work by shortening it, so the lid must be suspended from the frontalis muscle. A good Bell phenomenon is reassuring because frontalis suspension leaves lagophthalmos and the eye depends on that reflex for corneal protection. Levator resection is appropriate for moderate or good function, and Muller muscle conjunctival resection is reserved for mild ptosis with good function and a positive phenylephrine test.

Orbital decompression during the active inflammatory phase of thyroid eye disease is reserved for sight-threatening problems, principally dysthyroid compressive optic neuropathy that fails to respond to high-dose corticosteroids, and for severe corneal exposure from marked proptosis. Operating in the active phase otherwise risks unpredictable results because the deviation and proptosis are still changing. Diplopia and cosmetic rehabilitation are addressed once the disease has been inactive and stable for at least six months, and the correct sequence is decompression, then strabismus surgery, then eyelid surgery.

Full thickness eyelid defects of up to about one third of the lid margin can be closed directly, and in elderly patients with significant horizontal laxity even a half of the lid can often be apposed without tension. A semicircular Tenzel flap is added when direct closure is under tension, typically for defects of roughly one third to two thirds. A tarsoconjunctival flap from the upper lid, the Hughes procedure, is a staged reconstruction for large posterior lamellar defects exceeding two thirds and would be a considerable over-treatment here, with the added disadvantage of occluding the eye between stages.

A left hypertropia that the child compensates with a head tilt to the right is a left superior oblique palsy, since the deviation worsens on tilt toward the affected side and the patient tilts away from it. Absence of subjective excyclotorsion despite objective fundus torsion indicates a long-standing congenital palsy with sensory adaptation, which fits the chronic head posture and typically an overacting ipsilateral inferior oblique. Weakening the left inferior oblique, the direct antagonist, is the standard first procedure for a congenital superior oblique palsy with inferior oblique overaction and a deviation up to about 15 prism dioptres. Superior oblique tuck is reserved for a lax tendon, and operating on the vertical recti of the fellow right eye would be indicated only for larger or incomitant deviations after the oblique has been addressed.
concern: The source explanation field carries a stray fragment of a different question about neurofibromatosis, a transcription artifact. The item is also filed under oculoplastics although it is a strabismus question.

explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common eyelid malignancy and shows a strong predilection for the lower lid and medial canthus, appearing as a pearly nodule with rolled telangiectatic borders and central ulceration. Histologically the nests of basaloid cells show peripheral palisading of nuclei with retraction artifact from the surrounding stroma, which is essentially diagnostic. Squamous cell carcinoma is far less common on the lids, keratinises and shows intercellular bridges, sebaceous carcinoma favours the upper lid, masquerades as recurrent chalazion or unilateral blepharitis and shows pagetoid spread, and seborrhoeic keratosis is a benign stuck-on lesion with horn cysts.

Distichiasis is an accessory row of lashes emerging from the meibomian gland orifices along the posterior lid margin, arising from metaplasia of the sebaceous glands into hair follicles; it may be congenital, often autosomal dominant and associated with lymphoedema, or acquired after cicatrising conjunctival disease. Trichiasis by contrast is misdirection of lashes that arise from their normal anterior anatomical position. The other terms are not standard descriptors for this finding.

Conjunctival naevus is far more common than melanoma and is recognised histologically by well-circumscribed nests of bland melanocytes that mature and become smaller with increasing depth, by the absence of mitoses and pagetoid spread, and above all by the characteristic intralesional cystic epithelial inclusions containing goblet cells. Conjunctival melanoma instead shows atypical epithelioid or spindle cells invading the substantia propria with mitotic figures, frequently arising from adjacent primary acquired melanosis with atypia, and its thickness is measured precisely because tumours over about 2 mm carry a substantially worse prognosis for metastasis. Primary acquired melanosis is confined to the epithelium and would not form a measurable 2.4 mm thick mass.
concern: This item cannot be answered reliably from the text. The deciding features are the cytology and the presence or absence of epithelial inclusion cysts, which I cannot assess without the slide, and the fact that the question draws an arrow marking a 2.4 mm thickness is itself suspicious for a melanoma staging question, which is presumably why the source recorded doubt. I would not rely on this item without seeing the original image.

explanation: Hilar lymphadenopathy in a young African American patient with acute anterior uveitis is sarcoidosis, and the expected slit lamp finding is large greasy mutton-fat keratic precipitates on the inferior corneal endothelium in an Arlt triangle. These granulomatous precipitates are aggregates of macrophages and the epithelioid cells derived from them, in contrast to the fine keratic precipitates of non-granulomatous uveitis, which are composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils. Polymorphonuclear cells predominate in acute suppurative infection rather than in a chronic granulomatous deposit.
concern: Macrophages and epithelioid cells are effectively the same lineage, epithelioid cells being activated macrophages, so options A and C overlap and the intended distinction depends on the photograph. If the image showed iris granulomas such as Koeppe or Busacca nodules rather than keratic precipitates, epithelioid cells would be the better answer.

explanation: The Jackson cross cylinder sequence is to establish the best sphere, refine the cylinder axis, refine the cylinder power and then re-refine the sphere. The final step is necessary because each 0.50 dioptre change in minus cylinder power shifts the spherical equivalent by 0.25 dioptres, which must be compensated to keep the circle of least confusion on the retina. The duochrome test is a useful adjunct performed after the refraction is complete to check for over-minusing, and recording acuity is documentation rather than a refracting step.

By Prentice rule the induced prism equals the decentration in centimetres multiplied by the lens power in dioptres, so looking 1 cm below the optical centre induces 8 prism dioptres in the right eye and 4 in the left. Because both lenses are minus and the gaze is displaced in the same direction, both prisms are base down and therefore partially cancel between the eyes, leaving a net vertical imbalance of 4 prism dioptres. This anisometropic imbalance in downgaze is exactly why patients with unequal prescriptions struggle with reading through bifocals and why slab-off prism or separate reading glasses are prescribed.
